items.title: Section: Five Ways Concentration Is Actively Opposed, and Three Kinds of Solitude That Cure Them

items.zh: 復有五種定相違法。一、毀犯禁戒，二、無無間加行，三、無殷重加行，四、有沈沒，五、他所擾惱。復有三種遠離。一、住處遠離，二、見遠離，三、聞遠離。
items.en: There are also five dharmas opposed to concentration: transgressing the precepts, lacking uninterrupted effort, lacking earnest effort, the presence of sinking, and disturbance by others. There are also three kinds of solitude: solitude of place, solitude of view, and solitude of hearing.

items.title: Section: Five Weighty Faults That Burden the Purifying Mind

items.zh: 復次，心清淨行苾芻，略有五種等持相違厚重過失，能為定障。一、忿，二、慢，三、欲貪，四、薩迦耶見，五、不能堪忍。有五厚重三摩地相，由彼於此障礙而住，是故說名厚重過失。云何五相？
items.en: Furthermore, a monk practising purity of mind has, briefly, five weighty faults opposed to concentration, able to obstruct absorption: anger, pride, craving for sensual desire, the view of a real self, and inability to endure. There are five weighty characteristics of concentration which these faults obstruct by dwelling in opposition to them; this is why they are called weighty faults. What are the five characteristics?

items.title: Section: Five Weighty Qualities, and How Anger Alone Undoes Them

items.zh: 一者、獲得隨宜資具便生喜足；二者、好樂求諸善法；三、於身財無所顧戀；四、於生死及與涅槃，見大過失、最勝功德；五、於加行堪忍勤苦。此中忿者，謂懷忿故，若往他家不得利養，或得而少，或弊或遲，或不恭敬，由此便生顰蹙憤憾。從此因緣，發恚尋思及害尋思，多隨尋伺。彼由此故，先所未生勝三摩地不能得生。設彼已生還復退失。
items.en: First, contentment upon receiving whatever requisites are obtained. Second, delight in seeking every wholesome dharma. Third, no attachment towards body or wealth. Fourth, seeing great fault in birth and death and supreme virtue in nirvana. Fifth, patient endurance of hardship in effort. Among these, anger means that, holding anger, one who goes to another's house and receives no support, or little, or coarse, or slow, or disrespectful support, gives rise to a scowling resentment. From this cause, thoughts of malice and harm arise, dwelt upon repeatedly. Because of this, excellent concentration not yet arisen fails to arise, and if already arisen, falls away again.

items.title: Section: Pride That Refuses to Ask, and Craving That Contemplating the Body Can Cure

items.zh: 所言慢者，謂懷慢故，慢所制伏為性，於法不生恭敬，於諸師範尊重福田，不能時時身心卑屈敬問諮請：云何為善？云何不善？亦不勤求所有善法，由此不能解了引發三摩地義。從此因緣，發起輕慢相應尋思，多隨尋伺。彼由此故，先所未生，如前廣說。言欲貪者，謂懷貪故，多諸愛染，於身財等深生顧戀，由此於外五妙欲中多生散亂。從此因緣，生欲尋思、眷屬尋思、國土尋思、族望家勢相應尋思，多隨尋伺。彼由此故，先所未生，如前廣說。彼復不淨能為對治。應知不淨略有三相。謂糞穢相、彼等流相、能依所依差別相。
items.en: Pride means that, ruled by pride, one shows no reverence towards the Dharma, and cannot humbly and respectfully inquire of a teacher worthy of reverence what is wholesome and what is not, nor earnestly seek every wholesome dharma. Craving for sensual desire means that, holding much attachment, one deeply cherishes body and possessions, thereby scattering greatly among the five external objects of desire. Contemplating impurity serves as its antidote, briefly of three aspects: the mark of filth, the mark of filth's equal-flow, and the mark distinguishing the supported from its support.

items.title: Section: How the View of a Real Self Makes the Eight Worldly Winds Impossible to Release

items.zh: 薩迦耶見者，謂由身見制伏因緣，會遇世法，便為高欣、下慼塗染。設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。又即於彼世法眾相，親愛恒流之所漂溺。設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。
items.en: The view of a real self means that, controlled by the cause of self-view, one who encounters worldly conditions is stained by elation and dejection. Wishing to release this, one remains held back, opposed by self-view. And amid the many aspects of these same worldly conditions, one is drowned by the constant stream of affection. Wishing to release this, one remains held back, opposed by self-view.

items.zh: 又即世法眾相所生不正尋思之所燒惱。設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。又即於彼世法眾相追求之時，種種擾亂散動所逼。設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。又即由彼身見因緣，恒常執著世法所依無常諸取，由是因緣，為憂悲等之所逼惱。設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。又復即彼為欲除遣下地垢穢勤修善時，於彼加行不生喜樂。於此所治設欲棄捨，便為身見相違而住。如為除遣下地垢穢，為遣上地所有垢穢，當知亦爾。

items.title: Section: Four More Ways Self-View Holds On, and Why Enduring Hardship Matters

items.zh: 由此因故，雖作是心：我當於彼生死、涅槃，觀大過失、觀勝功德，便復顛倒。由此因緣，先雖獲得諸三摩地，然於未生聖諦現觀勝三摩地，不能得生。不堪忍者，謂懷不忍故，雖已獲得聖諦現觀勝三摩地，不能堪忍蚊虻等苦，捨離加行，多生懈怠。由此因緣，於所未生入根本定不能生起，設復已生還即退失。
items.en: Because of this cause, even while intending to see great fault in birth and death and supreme virtue in nirvana, this intention becomes inverted. Because of this, though various concentrations were previously attained, the transcendent concentration of direct realisation of the noble truths, not yet arisen, fails to arise. Inability to endure means that, holding this intolerance, even one who has attained the transcendent concentration of direct realisation of the noble truths cannot bear the suffering of mosquitoes and gnats, abandons sustained effort, and grows lazy. Because of this, root absorption not yet arisen fails to arise, and if already arisen, falls away again.

items.title: Section: Which Fault Blocks Which Stage, and Eight Reasons a Teacher Gives Up a Student

items.zh: 前三過失，能為最初三摩地障。次一過失，為諦現觀三摩地障。後一過失，為入根本三摩地障。復有差別。謂有八種棄捨近住弟子因緣，於彼雜染之所染污。由染污故，彼便棄捨近住弟子，非無煩惱諸阿羅漢常善住念有如斯事。
items.en: The first three faults obstruct only the earliest concentration. The next single fault obstructs the concentration of direct realisation of the noble truths. The last fault obstructs entering root concentration. There is a further distinction: eight causes for abandoning a resident student, arising from being stained by this same defilement, something that no arhat, free of affliction and ever well abiding in mindfulness, would ever do.

items.zh: 云何為八？謂性於彼近住弟子有憎惡心，唯欲自身受於恭敬；如欲恭敬，欲受利養亦復如是；近住弟子多所毀犯、行不正行；又於近住諸弟子眾饒益損減，便有所須及與不須；於增上戒教授折伏不能堪忍；於增上心、增上慧住教授折伏不能堪忍；於營眾務所有擾惱不能堪忍。

blocks.text: Fascicle 63 continues the Stage of Concentration: what blocks it, and why self-view makes the "eight worldly winds" so hard to let go of.

Master Cháng Bǎi: without practising calm and insight continuously and earnestly, one cannot attain concentration. When sinking arises, the object is not clear. Three kinds of solitude cure this; for example, dwelling where one is less disturbed.
Master Cháng Bǎi: from the side of what obstructs, the obstruction is strong; from the side of what is obstructed, the merit is firm.

Master Cháng Bǎi: in the effort of calm and insight, one endures the hardship that comes with diligence. Thinking wrongly that an offering came too slowly obstructs concentration, and anger can make concentration already won fall away.
Master Cháng Bǎi: controlled by pride, one cannot be humble and does not ask questions. Contemplation of impurity counters craving: food is filth before it changes, and filth is food after.

Master Cháng Bǎi: meeting loss, slander, censure, or pain, the mind sinks in distress, because it has not seen through the self. (Untranslated, 0648c14: burned by wrong thoughts arising from worldly things, harried while chasing them, distressed by clinging to what is impermanent, joyless in the effort to clear lower stains: in each case, wishing to let go, one is held back by self-view.)
Master Cháng Bǎi: though the path is achieved, one may still be unable to bear mosquito bites; laziness comes from this.

Master Cháng Bǎi: self-view obstructs transcendent concentration. An arhat, always mindful, would not fall. (Untranslated, 0649a08: eight reasons a teacher gives up a student: the teacher's own dislike and wish for honour and gain; the student's many violations; whether the students help or burden; and the teacher's inability to bear instructing them in discipline, mind, and wisdom, or the troubles of community work.)
The list of reasons a teacher gives up a student is notably honest: half of them are the teacher's faults.

quiz.q: What are the five dharmas opposed to concentration?
options: transgressing the precepts, lacking uninterrupted effort, lacking earnest effort, sinking, and disturbance by others
anger, pride, craving for sensual desire, the view of a real self, and inability to endure
sensual desire, ill will, dullness and sleep, restlessness and regret, and doubt
arrogance, unwillingness, disbelief, distraction, and confusion
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: not practising calm and insight without interruption, or not earnestly and thoroughly, one cannot attain concentration. Option B lists the five weighty faults that come next in the treatise, and C the five hindrances.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain the presence of sinking?
options: in practising calm and insight, sinking arises and the object does not appear clearly
the mind flows outward after other objects and cannot return to the original one at all
regret over broken precepts weighs the mind down
disturbance by others makes the mind angry
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: when sinking arises in calm and insight, the object is not clearly present, and this obstructs concentration. Flowing outward belongs to restlessness rather than to sinking, and each of the five obstacles has a distinct role.

quiz.q: Which three kinds of solitude does the treatise list?
options: solitude of body, of mind, and of speech, following the three karmas
solitude from crowds, bad friends, and gain
solitude of place, of view, and of hearing
solitude from the three realms in turn
quiz.why: The treatise names only these three. Master Cháng Bǎi on the first: dwelling where meditation is less disturbed avoids disturbance by others and many troubles. His definitions of the other two are not firm, so only the names are tested.

quiz.q: What are the five weighty faults opposed to concentration?
options: transgressing precepts, lacking uninterrupted or earnest effort, sinking, and disturbance by others
anger, pride, craving for sensual desire, the view of a real self, and inability to endure
flattery, deceit, pretence, deception, shamelessness
faithlessness, laziness, forgetfulness, lack of concentration, wrong wisdom
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: in brief, five things oppose concentration and keep a practitioner from absorption. These five differ from the five dharmas opposed to concentration in §1, and from the secondary afflictions of the previous fascicle.

quiz.q: Which is one of the five weighty characteristics of concentration?
options: seeking better requisites after receiving whatever is obtained
carefully protecting body and wealth
seeing virtue in birth and death and fault in nirvana
patient endurance of hardship in effort
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: in the effort of calm and insight, one endures the hardship that comes with diligence. The other options reverse the marks of contentment, of non-attachment to body and wealth, and of seeing fault in birth and death.

quiz.q: How does one holding anger who gets no support come to obstruct concentration, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: resentment produces thoughts of malice and harm, which are wrong reflection and obstruct concentration
without food the body is too weak, so one must first secure enough support
the donor's scolding costs one's reputation
finding other donors leaves no time
quiz.why: The treatise gives the slow or lacking offering as the occasion. Master Cháng Bǎi: this is wrong reflection; with wrong deliberation, concentration is obstructed. The hindrance lies in the anger and the thoughts it produces, not in physical hunger.

quiz.q: What does the treatise say of one ruled by pride towards teachers and fields of merit?
options: one visits them often while inwardly comparing, seeming respectful
one cannot humbly and respectfully inquire of them what is wholesome and what is not
one grows angry and slanders them
one abandons them for outside teachers
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: one is controlled by pride, and the mind follows it, and cannot often be humble in body and mind. The treatise then adds that one does not earnestly seek wholesome dharmas. The further consequences of pride are missing from the English.

quiz.q: What three aspects of impurity does the treatise list as the antidote to craving?
options: bruised, festering, and skeletal corpses, the usual contemplation stages
the marks of suffering, emptiness, impermanence
inner body, outer body, and both
the mark of filth, its outflow, and the mark distinguishing supported from support
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: contemplation of impurity counters the affliction of craving. The treatise names three aspects. The lecture reports several schools on what each means, especially the supported and the support, so only the names are tested.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain being stained by elation and dejection on meeting worldly conditions?
options: one's status rises and falls by karma, with no connection to self-view
meeting the eight worldly conditions, the mind sinks in dejection at loss, not seeing that situations are like illusions
one delights in higher realms and grieves in lower ones
one's meditation rises and falls
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: on meeting the eight worldly conditions, when loss, slander, censure, or pain appears, the mind sinks in distress, because it has not seen through situations as illusions or known that no self can be found.

quiz.q: What does the treatise say of one who cannot endure, though having attained direct realisation?
options: having seen the truths one feels no pain at all, so intolerance is only for ordinary beings
one loses realisation and returns to ordinary status
unable to bear mosquitoes and gnats, one abandons effort, grows lazy, and root absorption fails or falls away
one turns to seek heaven instead of meditation
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: though the noble path is achieved, one cannot bear mosquito bites; laziness comes from this inability to endure. Realisation of the truths is not lost, but root absorption does not arise, or falls away if it had arisen.

quiz.q: Which concentration does each group of the five faults obstruct?
options: the first three root concentration, the next the earliest, and the last direct realisation
the first three the earliest concentration, the next direct realisation, and the last root concentration
all five the earliest concentration
all five direct realisation
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the next fault is the view of self, the obstacle to transcendent concentration of realisation; the last obstructs entering the four meditations. So anger, pride, and craving come first, and the order of the faults follows the stages of practice.

quiz.q: This is rendered "obstruct only the earliest concentration." What is added?
options: nothing: the three matter only at the start, so "only" makes this clear, as the lecture says here
"earliest" is added
"only": the text has no such word, and §3 says anger also makes attained concentration fall away
"faults" is added
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: they obstruct the first attainment of concentration. But §3 says of anger that concentration already arisen falls away, so "only" goes beyond the Chinese and contradicts the earlier passage.
